A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GRADMM, with matching core methods, experiments and appendices. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison; the convergence proofs, prompts and generated examples can be matched across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments, cross-model transfer results, component ablations and generated-text examples in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds differential-privacy evaluations, membership-inference results, gradient and distribution analyses, and additional benchmark results.

M1.justification: New Section 4.5 extends GRADMM with per-example gradient clipping and Gaussian noise added to the averaged target gradient. Algorithm 1 incorporates privacy parameters into optimization. This changes the gradient-matching procedure, while retaining the ADMM updates, top-k projection and filtering.

E1.justification: Appendix D and Figure 7 extend the existing data-scarce sentiment-classification evaluation to IMDB and a reported Sentence polarity benchmark. Section 5.3 also adds an SST-2 membership-inference test. The PDFs do not clarify whether Sentence polarity represents distinct data from the retained Rotten tomatoes benchmark.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain zero-shot generation, few-shot generation, Herding, K-center and Random comparisons. Added diagnostics reuse existing comparators or real data; different privacy settings are variants of GRADMM rather than newly introduced comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds privacy-controlled evaluations using epsilon values 0.05, 4 and infinity, delta 0.0001 and clipping threshold 1, plus normalized-gradient, FID and nearest-example-distance measurements. Its new membership-inference protocol selects a threshold on 100 members and 100 non-members, then evaluates another balanced group. Existing fine-tuning budgets and checkpoint-selection rules remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendix D add gradient-error trajectories, distribution matching measured by FID, nearest-training-example distance histograms, membership-inference attacks and privacy-budget sensitivity. These examine gradient alignment, representativeness, copying and privacy–utility tradeoffs. The original projection, last-layer and filtering ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 gives point accuracies without uncertainty or repeated-run information. v2 adds ± values throughout Table 1, shaded uncertainty bands in Figure 1, and membership-inference averages over 10 runs. Classification run counts and the meanings of the ± values and bands remain unspecified; an increase in runs for existing experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and Figure 1 contain revised results and new private-GRADMM results. For example, five-example SST-2 accuracy changes from 87.0 to 86.5±0.5 for non-private GRADMM, with 84.2±0.1 newly reported for epsilon 0.05. v2 also adds privacy, FID, gradient and benchmark outcomes. Table 2 and the original ablation values remain unchanged. The revised Table 1 supports the text's 13.1-point maximum advantage, although its caption retains 10.4%.

T1.justification: Section 4.5 extends the formal scope to differential privacy, specifying piecewise noise calibration in epsilon and delta and invoking composition to claim an (epsilon, delta)-DP guarantee. The convergence assumptions, Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3 and their Appendix A proofs remain unchanged; no separate privacy proof is added there.

C1.justification: Although v1 already describes GRADMM as privacy-preserving, v2 strengthens this into an explicit differential-privacy contribution. Its abstract and introduction now claim privacy guarantees alongside convergence and performance guarantees, and its conclusion emphasizes matching noisy target gradients. Readability and transferability claims are retained.

C2.justification: v2 interprets gradient alignment and distribution similarity as explanations for performance, distance histograms as evidence against copying, and membership-inference results as privacy evidence even without DP. It newly qualifies effectiveness as dependent on real-example diversity and hypothesizes that privacy noise can improve generalization when only five real examples are available.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, documents privacy parameters and attack procedures, and explains that synthetic examples are generated independently. The independent-generation remark is additional documentation rather than an established procedural change. Existing optimization settings, hardware information and Appendix B prompts are retained; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting differential privacy, noise calibration, membership inference, noise-related generalization and IMDB, while removing the Dubey et al. Llama reference. Section 2 also removes the blanket statement that dataset distillation preserves privacy. The broader positioning against existing text-distillation and generation approaches remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted abstract, introduction and conclusion edits, inserts privacy and analysis subsections and Appendix D, and adds an impact statement and acknowledgements. It also updates affiliation and publication text and shortens some baseline explanations. Most existing prose and the overall narrative organization are retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a privacy-setting column and uncertainty displays, and Figure 1 gains private-GRADMM curves and shaded bands. v2 adds the FID table and substantial new plots in Figures 2 and 7–10. Existing ablation tables, sample-text figures and prompt figures are retained with relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's weakly supported privacy assurances by supplying an explicit clipping-and-noise mechanism, privacy settings and attack evaluations. New gradient and distribution analyses directly test important explanations for the method's effectiveness, while uncertainty reporting improves assessment of the main results. The privacy argument remains brief, statistical definitions are incomplete and Table 1 has a stale caption, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidential support.
